title: The Pond That Looked Empty

passage: When our science group first visited the new pond, we thought the project had failed. We could not see a single frog, and the water looked still. title: Soup from the Spare Vegetables
objective: CEFR-inspired sample lesson: explain how a community food project balances two practical needs.
passage: Our community café began making Friday soup with vegetables that local shops had not sold. The vegetables were still good to eat, although some looked unusual. title: Who Is the Wildlife Camera For?
objective: CEFR-inspired sample lesson: evaluate competing arguments and draw a qualified inference from limited evidence.
passage: A camera above the school garden streamed pictures of nesting birds to classroom screens. Within a week, students who had never visited the garden were asking thoughtful questions about the birds. The nature club called this an educational success and proposed a second camera beside another nest. The caretaker was less enthusiastic. Installing the first camera had required several visits, and she had noticed the birds waiting nearby rather than entering the nest while people were present. No one knew whether this brief delay had caused a lasting problem. At a meeting, one student argued that any disturbance made the project unacceptable; another said that growing interest justified it. The science teacher suggested a third option: keep watching the existing camera, but postpone new installations until the nesting season ended. The club accepted this proposal, although it would mean fewer pictures this term. Its newsletter described the decision as 'giving our curiosity a timetable'.
listeningPassage: Our class compared two paths through the woodland. More birds were heard beside the quieter path, so several students wanted the busy path closed. However, the quiet route also had taller trees and was visited earlier in the morning. We could not separate these differences from the effect of noise. The park volunteer suggested repeating the counts at matching times and recording the types of trees along each route. Until then, she supported asking visitors to speak softly near nesting areas, but she did not think our results alone justified closing a whole path.

title: When Reusable Means Used Again
objective: CEFR-inspired sample lesson: assess a sustainability claim and distinguish a promising idea from demonstrated results.
passage: For its summer fair, Brook School replaced disposable drink cups with durable ones. Visitors paid a small deposit, which they received back when they returned a cup. The organisers proudly ordered only one bin for cup waste. By the end of the fair, however, forty of the two hundred cups were missing. Some visitors had taken them home as souvenirs; others had left them near the playing field because the return desk was beside the entrance. A poster later announced that the fair had become 'waste-free'. The eco committee challenged that description. Fewer cups had been thrown into bins, but the team had not recorded how much washing was needed or whether the missing cups would be used again. For the next event, the committee proposed several clearly marked return points and a count of cups across the whole site. title: Untidy on Purpose
objective: CEFR-inspired sample lesson: interpret an implicit stance and synthesise ecological and community priorities in an appropriate register.
passage:
When the park team stopped mowing a strip beside the playground, complaints arrived before the first flowers did. A residents' newsletter described the strip as 'an experiment in forgetting the lawnmower'. The nature club replied with a list of insects found there, assuming that evidence of wildlife would settle the matter. It did not. Some residents were concerned about the narrow path; others simply associated long grass with a place nobody cared for.

At a public meeting, the gardener resisted both descriptions. The strip was neither abandoned nor guaranteed to become a miniature paradise, she said. Different plants would appear over time, and the team would need to observe what actually grew. She proposed widening the mown edge and putting up a small sign explaining the maintenance plan. title: The Perfectly Imperfect Carrot
objective: CEFR-inspired sample lesson: identify an implied criticism and reconcile persuasive language with a fair account of evidence.
passage:
At the school market, a stall sold bent carrots under the cheerful slogan 'Too quirky to waste'. Students had rescued them from a grower's surplus, and the first boxes sold quickly. Encouraged by the response, the team designed bright packaging and raised the price slightly to cover it. Their report celebrated a change in attitudes: shoppers were apparently learning that appearance mattered less than taste.

A parent who regularly bought inexpensive loose vegetables was not entirely convinced. 'I am glad these carrots found a home,' she wrote, 'though I hope being ordinary will not become their next disadvantage.' Some students thought she was objecting to the project itself. Their business mentor read the comment differently. The parent might be questioning whether the stall had made unusual appearance into a new selling point, rather than making shoppers less concerned with appearance overall.

The team tested this possibility at the next market. Half the carrots were sold loose with a plain explanation of their origin; half retained the decorated boxes. Shoppers could choose either, and the team recorded their reasons. The results were mixed: packaging attracted attention, but several customers valued being able to buy exactly the amount they needed. The revised report described successful sales and a promising discussion, while leaving the larger claim about changed attitudes open.

objective: CEFR-inspired sample lesson: interpret institutional language and synthesise conflicting uses into a qualified proposal.
passage:
The school announced that its little-used study room would become a 'flexible learning hub'. The proposal mentioned movable tables, craft materials and a small recording booth. In the announcement, flexibility seemed to promise something for everyone. During consultation, however, students who used the room for quiet reading discovered that their preferred activity appeared only under 'other possible uses'.

The project team said that nothing had been ruled out. It also explained that the new equipment required regular bookings to justify its cost. A librarian observed that quiet study rarely generated bookings: students came when they needed it, sometimes for only ten minutes. Counting reservations would therefore make one type of use highly visible and another almost disappear.

The student paper initially planned the headline 'School abolishes silence'. After interviewing the team, its editor chose a less dramatic title: 'What will flexibility leave room for?' The article accepted the value of making and recording, but questioned whether all uses could coexist merely because the furniture moved. It proposed protected quiet periods and a review that included informal visitors as well as booked groups.

The team welcomed the article as a 'helpful contribution to an evolving plan'. The editor was pleased to see the issue acknowledged, though she noted that no quiet periods had yet appeared on the draft timetable.

title: The Fox That Declined the Invitation
objective: CEFR-inspired sample lesson: analyse rhetorical framing and reformulate a nuanced argument without losing its qualifications.
passage:
For the school nature trail, the publicity team chose a fox as its unofficial host. On posters, a cheerful drawing welcomed visitors to 'my woodland home'; online, a series of photographs promised an encounter with the real animal. The fox, having contributed nothing to these arrangements, ceased appearing near the trail shortly before opening day. Volunteers worried that visitors would feel cheated.

One suggested moving the camera to find the fox's new route. Another proposed replacing the photographs with an account of the signs it left behind. The discussion might have remained a practical matter had a student not asked when an invitation to notice wildlife had become a promise that wildlife would perform.

The publicity team defended the campaign: a recognisable character had persuaded families to explore a place they previously ignored. This was a reasonable point, the student conceded. Stories could open a door. Her objection was to quietly treating the story's convenience as a requirement the animal should meet. A fox made approachable on paper was still entitled, in the ordinary rather than legal sense, to remain elusive in the woods.

The revised trail kept the illustrated host but removed the promise of a sighting. At its entrance stood a new notice: 'Our guide may be elsewhere today. The woodland is still here.' Some visitors found this charming; a few asked where to get a better photograph. In the project review, the student resisted calling the missing fox a failure. It had exposed a weakness in the invitation, she wrote, and perhaps improved the kind of attention the trail was asking for.

title: The Trouble with a Perfect Score
objective: CEFR-inspired sample lesson: interpret irony, weigh competing definitions of success, and produce a precise synthesis.
passage:
The canteen's campaign began with a slogan no one wished to oppose: 'Every scrap counts.' For a month, pupils weighed the food returned on their trays, and a graph by the entrance showed the total falling. The campaign team announced that the school was approaching its goal of zero waste. Its neat downward line became the preferred illustration for every presentation.

Yet the graph had acquired responsibilities it was not designed to carry. The kitchen had reduced portion sizes after several pupils requested lighter lunches, while a new fruit stall outside school had changed how hungry some pupils were on arrival. Neither development made the figures false. They did, however, complicate the claim that the campaign alone had transformed everyone's habits.

When a pupil suggested adding these details to the display, an organiser worried that qualifications would drain the message of energy. 'We finally have a story people understand,' she said. The pupil replied that a story need not become less useful merely because it became less tidy. He also questioned whether zero was the right ambition for every tray: trying an unfamiliar vegetable might produce a little waste on the way to a broader diet.

The final display kept the graph but placed it beside an explanation of what it could and could not show. The slogan survived, now followed by 'and so do the reasons'. In the campaign review, the organiser called this a compromise. The pupil preferred to call it a more demanding version of success: a school able to reduce waste without rewarding the avoidance of lunch.
listeningPassage: Our school shop tried giving reusable lunch boxes a score based on how many disposable wrappers they appeared to replace. One pupil pointed out that she already carried lunch in an old container, so buying the new box would improve her score without changing her habits. The organisers realised they were rewarding a visible purchase more readily than an existing practice. They revised the activity so pupils could describe what they already did and identify a useful next step. A teacher welcomed the change but cautioned against simply replacing a purchase competition with a competition in persuasive self-description. The revised activity therefore asked for a modest, observable example over several days, while making clear that the aim was reflection rather than a ranking of whose family was most virtuous.

title: Who Gets to Sound Like a Leader?
objective: CEFR-inspired sample lesson: recognise implicit assumptions in evaluative language and reformulate a balanced position precisely.
passage:
When the student council introduced a leadership award, its guidance praised pupils who 'speak with confidence and bring others with them'. The phrase sounded generous enough to pass without discussion. At the first selection meeting, however, the nominations clustered around students who spoke readily in assemblies. A pupil who had quietly reorganised the lunchtime library rota was praised for being helpful, then moved to a different category.

The librarian asked whether this distinction described the pupils' contributions or merely the forms in which those contributions became visible. The rota had survived several disagreements because its organiser asked precise questions, checked who would be affected and changed her proposal. She rarely delivered a polished speech. The panel chair agreed that these were valuable qualities, but worried that broadening the criteria would make almost any cooperative act count as leadership.

In an editorial, the student paper resisted both an easy reversal and the original formula. Confident speaking was not a fault, it argued, and quietness was no certificate of wisdom. The problem was allowing one recognisable style to stand in for the judgement the award claimed to honour. The editorial proposed asking what a pupil had enabled others to do, and how they had handled disagreement, before considering how persuasive the account sounded.

The panel adopted the questions but retained confidence in its guidance, now defined partly as a willingness to revise a view. Some students called this a contradiction. The librarian called it a useful inconvenience: the word could no longer do the panel's thinking for it.
listeningPassage: In a workshop on peer feedback, students compared two comments on a presentation. One said, 'You seemed completely certain'; the other said, 'You made it clear which conclusions the evidence supported.' Several students preferred the first because it sounded more enthusiastic. The tutor asked them to imagine a presentation containing an unanswered question. Under the first comment, acknowledging the gap might look like a weakness; under the second, it could be part of a strong performance. She was not suggesting that hesitation automatically signalled thoughtfulness, or that fluent delivery concealed shallow ideas. Rather, feedback should identify the achievement it intended to praise. The group rewrote its checklist to include clear delivery, appropriate confidence and explicit limits. One student observed that this was less convenient than awarding a single mark for 'presence'. The tutor agreed: convenience was useful until it began deciding what the class was able to notice.
